title.zh: 卡爾巴拉：侯賽因之殉難

region.en: Karbala, on the Euphrates, Iraq (literal pin)
region.zh: 伊拉克幼發拉底河畔卡爾巴拉（實際定位）

texts.period: Event 680 CE; English: S. Ockley, History of the Saracens (Bohn ed. 1890); W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 25

source.work: Simon Ockley, The History of the Saracens (Bohn ed. 1890); William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 25

texts.license: Public domain (English editions 1890-91; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Yazid is proclaimed caliph at Damascus; Husayn, grandson of the Prophet, refuses the oath and rides for Kufa. He is met by the army of Ubaydullah ibn Ziyad at Karbala, cut off from the Euphrates, and besieged for days without water. On the day of Ashura the seventy-two are struck down one by one; Husayn falls last, with his infant son in his arms. Zaynab carries the captives to Damascus, and the mourning for the family of the Prophet becomes the rite of Muharram.
summary.zh: 大馬士革擁立耶齊德為哈里發；先知之孫侯賽因拒誓，騎向庫法。於卡爾巴拉遇伊本·齊亞德之軍，被截於幼發拉底河之外，斷水圍困多日。阿舒拉之日，七十二人逐一被殺；侯賽因殿後而歿，懷中抱其幼子。宰乃布攜俘至大馬士革；先知家屬之哀悼成為穆哈蘭月之儀。

sensitivity.note: The martyrdom of Husayn is a cardinal devotion of Shi'ism and a grief-event in Sunni memory alike; recorded as the received narrative of Tabari/Ockley without sectarian framing.

passages.text: On the death of Mu'awiya his son Yazid was proclaimed caliph at Damascus. Husayn, the son of Ali and the grandson of the Prophet, refused the oath and rode from Medina towards Kufa, whose people had written to invite him. The governor Ubaydullah ibn Ziyad sent an army against him; his path was turned aside, and he was met at the plain of Karbala, two days from the Euphrates.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Ockley (1890) and Muir (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Husayn was besieged with his family and companions — seventy-two fighting men, among them his brother Abbas and his young son — and the water of the river was denied them. On the tenth day of Muharram, the day of Ashura, they were struck down one after another; Abbas fell at the water, and the infant of Husayn died in his father's arms, an arrow through its neck. Husayn fell last, faint with thirst, crying the old cry: 'Is there any helper?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Ockley (1890); not verbatim.

passages.text: His head was carried to Ibn Ziyad and then to Damascus; his sister Zaynab led the captives, and in the court of Yazid she spoke the protest that the tradition remembers. The mourning for the family of the Prophet — the weeping processions of Muharram, the ta'ziya recitations, the shrines of Karbala and Najaf — grew out of the plain where the seventy-two died; and the Sunni calendar keeps the tenth of Muharram as a fast of grief and of the Ark's resting alike.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the aftermath as told in Ockley (1890) and the Arabic historians; not verbatim.

title.en: Al-Mansur and the Death of Abu Muslim
title.zh: 曼蘇爾與阿布·穆斯林之死

region.en: Kufa and the Khurasan road (symbolic pin at Baghdad)
region.zh: 庫法與呼羅珊道（象徵性定位於巴格達）

texts.period: Event 755 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 39
texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Abu Muslim, the maker of the Abbasid revolution, has won Persia with the black banners. The caliph al-Mansur summons him to the court; the amir is warned, and comes. The caliph reproaches him with the name of Abu Muslim — 'Art thou Abu Muslim? I will make thee a prey to the dogs of the streets' — and the bodyguard does the rest. The revolution devours its maker; and Persia murmurs for twenty years.
summary.zh: 阿拔斯革命的締造者阿布·穆斯林已以黑旗得波斯。哈里發曼蘇爾召其入廷；封臣受警，仍前來。哈里發以『阿布·穆斯林』之名責之——『你是阿布·穆斯林嗎？我必使你為街犬之食』——衛士續行其事。革命吞其締造者；波斯怨憤二十年。

sensitivity.note: Early Abbasid historiography as received in Muir.

passages.text: Abu Muslim had made the Abbasid revolution in Khurasan and won Persia for the House. The caliph al-Mansur, grown uneasy before so great a man, summoned him to the court. The friends of Abu Muslim warned him; the astrologers warned him; and he came, saying that he had given thirty years to the House and would not refuse its summons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 39; not verbatim.

passages.text: He entered and saluted; the caliph reproached him, and then spoke the word the historians have kept: 'Art thou Abu Muslim? I will make thee a prey to the dogs of the streets.' The bodyguard closed; and the maker of the dynasty was slain in the caliph's tent. Persia murmured for twenty years after, and the sects that remembered him raised him to a hidden lord.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 39; not verbatim.

title.en: Al-Mansur Founds Baghdad: The Round City

region.zh: 底格里斯河渡口的巴格達（實際定位）

texts.period: Founded 762 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 38
texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The caliph chooses the crossing of the Tigris and Sarat canals near the old Persian villages — 'a market for all the world, and nothing that the river brings can get past it.' Four thousand architects measure a city of concentric walls, Khuld the 'Eternal'; the trench is dug, the foundations laid of burned brick in rows of reed — 'O God, Thou art the Everlasting Lord; build Thou for me.' In four years the Round City stands, and it is called Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace.
summary.zh: 哈里發擇底格里斯河與薩拉特運河交匯處，近古波斯村落——『天下之市集，河所載者無不經此』。四千名建築師量畫同心圓牆之城，名『永恆』（胡爾德）；掘溝，以蘆葦為行、焙磚為基——『主啊，你是永活之主；為我而建吧』。四年之間圓城立，名『和平之城』（麥地那·薩拉姆）。

sensitivity.note: Early Abbasid historiography; the founding is a landmark of urban and intellectual history.

passages.text: Al-Mansur sought a site for his capital and chose the crossing of the Tigris and the Sarat canals, by the villages of the old Persian name — a market for all the world, he said, with nothing that the river brings able to pass it. He had the ground measured by his engineers: a city of two concentric walls with a ditch between, the mosque and the palace at the centre under a golden dome.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 38; not verbatim.

passages.text: The trench was dug first, the caliph himself striking the first earth and praying: 'O God, Thou art the Everlasting Lord; build Thou for me; the world passes and Thy kingdom abides.' The walls were of burned brick laid in rows of reeds, the gates of iron; and in four years the Round City stood, called Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace — and under its caliphs it became the seat of the translation of the sciences and of the lore of the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 38; not verbatim.

title.en: Harun al-Rashid and the Fall of the Barmecides
title.zh: 哈倫·拉希德與巴爾馬克家族之傾覆

region.zh: 巴格達哈倫宮廷（實際定位）

texts.period: Event 803 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 46
texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Ja'far the Barmecide, vizier and playmate of Harun, is suddenly commanded to death; the tale is told that the caliph, feasting, had promised the hand of his sister Abbasa to Ja'far in jest, and that the jest was taken for a marriage. Whatever the cause, the sentence is carried in a night: Ja'far is struck in the hall of justice, his father Yahya cast into prison, the palaces of the family stripped. 'The cup of the Barmecides,' the Persian proverb runs, 'is broken.'
summary.zh: 巴爾馬克家族的賈法爾——哈倫的大臣與少年友伴——忽奉死命；相傳哈里發宴中戲許其妹阿巴西之婚，而戲言成真。無論其因，一夕行刑：賈法爾於議政廳被誅，其父葉海雅下獄，家族宮邸盡抄。波斯諺云：『巴爾馬克之杯已碎。』

sensitivity.note: Abbasid court historiography; the fall of the Barmecides is a locus classicus of the Arabic anecdote tradition.

passages.text: Ja'far the Barmecide had been the vizier of Harun al-Rashid and the companion of his boyhood; the House of Barmak had governed the East for a generation. In the year 803 the caliph commanded his death suddenly, without public cause; the tale is told that he had promised the hand of his sister Abbasa in jest at a feast, and that the jest had been taken for a marriage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 46; not verbatim.

passages.text: The sentence was carried in a night: Ja'far was struck in the hall of justice, and his head sent to Baghdad; his father Yahya and his brother Fadl were cast into prison; the palaces of the family were stripped of their stuff. The Persian proverb kept the memory: 'The cup of the Barmecides is broken' — and the anecdote lore of the Arabs made the fall of the great House a byword for the turn of the king's favour.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 46; not verbatim.

title.en: The Brothers' War: Amin and Ma'mun

region.en: Baghdad and Merv (symbolic pin at Baghdad)
region.zh: 巴格達與梅爾夫（象徵性定位於巴格達）

texts.period: Events 809-813 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 47
texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Harun divides the empire on his deathbed: Amin to reign at Baghdad, Ma'mun to hold Khurasan beyond the passes. The brothers' peace breaks; the Tahirid armies come west, Baghdad is besieged for a year, and Amin is taken in the last sally and slain on a bridge of boats. Ma'mun reigns from Merv, and the House is split between the two capitals for years.
summary.zh: 哈倫臨終分帝國：阿敏都於巴格達，馬蒙轄山外的呼羅珊。兄弟之約破裂；塔希爾軍西來，巴格達被圍一年，阿敏於最後的突圍中被擒，死於船橋之上。馬蒙自梅爾夫執政；王朝於兩都之間分裂数年。

sensitivity.note: Abbasid historiography as received in Muir.

passages.text: Harun al-Rashid on his deathbed divided his empire: Amin to reign at Baghdad, and Ma'mun to hold Khurasan beyond the passes, with his own guard and treasury. The peace of the brothers lasted as long as the guardians appointed; then Amin took the succession to himself, and Ma'mun refused, and the armies of Khurasan came west under Tahir.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 47; not verbatim.

passages.text: Baghdad was besieged for a year, house by house, the palaces burned and the people starved. In the last sally Amin was taken in a boat, and was slain on a bridge of the river by the men of Tahir; his head was sent to Merv. Ma'mun reigned from Khurasan, and did not come to Baghdad for years; and the House that Harun had divided never wholly joined again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 47; not verbatim.

title.en: Tariq Crosses to the Rock of Gibraltar
title.zh: 塔里克渡至直布羅陀之岩

region.zh: 直布羅陀與加的斯海岸（實際定位）

texts.period: Event 711 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37 (Spanish conquest); S. Ockley (1890)

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37; Simon Ockley, History of the Saracens (1890)

texts.license: Public domain (English editions 1890-91; Arabic originals 10th-11th centuries)

summary.en: Tariq ibn Ziyad crosses from Morocco to the rock that bears his name with seven thousand Berbers, and burns the boats: 'Where can you flee? The sea is behind you, the enemy in front.' Roderick the Visigoth comes against him with the hosts of Spain; the battle lasts a week, and the Visigothic kingdom falls. The rock keeps the commander's name; and Spain passes to the Muslims for eight hundred years.
summary.zh: 塔里克·本·齊亞德率七千柏柏爾人自摩洛哥渡至以他為名的岩地，並焚其舟：『你們能逃往何處？海在你身後，敵在你面前。』西哥特王羅德里克率西班牙大軍迎擊；戰事持續一週，西哥特王國傾覆。岩留統帥之名；西班牙歸穆斯林八百年。

sensitivity.note: Andalusi historiography as received in Muir/Ockley from Arabic sources.

passages.text: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from Morocco to the great rock of the strait with seven thousand Berbers, and burned the boats behind him. He spoke to them, in the speech the historians have kept: 'Whither can you flee? The sea is behind you, the enemy before you; you have nothing left but truth and courage.' And the rock took his name — Jabal Tariq, Gibraltar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Arabic accounts via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37; not verbatim.

passages.text: Roderick, the last Visigothic king, came against him with the hosts of Spain. The battle lasted a week on the river of the south; the king fled or was drowned in the Guadalquivir, and his kingdom fell with him. The cities of Spain opened their gates one after another, and for eight hundred years the land of the Visigoths was the land of the Muslims, and its capital became Cordoba.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Arabic accounts via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37; not verbatim.

title.en: Abd al-Rahman and the Palm of Ronda
title.zh: 阿布杜·拉赫曼與隆達的棕櫚

region.zh: 安達魯西亞隆達（實際定位）

texts.period: Event c. 756 CE; the poem preserved in Ibn Abd Rabbih's Arabic anthology; retold in later European histories

source.work: The palm-tree anecdote from the Arabic tradition (Ibn Abd Rabbih, al-Iqd al-Farid; retold in European histories of Spain); Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 38

texts.license: Public domain (Arabic originals medieval; English edition 1891)

summary.en: The Umayyad prince Abd al-Rahman, sole survivor of the massacre of his house, lands in Spain and builds his kingdom at Cordoba. Riding in the country of Ronda he finds a palm tree, the first he has seen since Damascus; he lays hold of it and speaks the lines the anthologies have kept: 'A palm like me, in exile far from home, parted from people and children... Turn to me, O palm, and hear me cry: as we are far from our people, so are you from yours.'
summary.zh: 伍麥葉王子阿布杜·拉赫曼——其家被屠之唯一倖存者——登陸西班牙，建都於科爾多瓦。行於隆達之鄉，見一棕櫚，乃其自大馬士革以來所見首株；他執其幹，誦出後世文集所存之句：『如我之棕櫚，離鄉萬里，與族人子女相隔……棕櫚啊，轉向我，聽我呼喊：我們離族人甚遠，你亦離你的族人甚遠。』

sensitivity.note: Anecdote lore of the Umayyad exiles of Spain; the palm poem is among the most quoted texts of Andalusi tradition.

passages.text: Abd al-Rahman ibn Mu'awiya, the sole survivor of the Umayyad house after the Abbasid massacre, fled across half the world to Spain, and built his kingdom at Cordoba. Riding in the country of Ronda, he saw a palm tree — the first since Damascus — and laid hold of it, and spoke:
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote and poem as preserved in the Arabic anthologies; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'A palm like me, in exile far from home, parted from people and children, from kindred and from land: turn to me, O palm, and hear me cry — as we are far from our people, so are you from yours.' And the men of Spain wept to see their prince weep for a tree; and the kingdom of the exiles of Cordoba stood for three hundred years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote and poem as preserved in the Arabic anthologies; not verbatim.

region.en: Alamut fortress, Elburz mountains, Persia (literal pin)
region.zh: 波斯厄爾布爾士山阿拉穆特要塞（實際定位）

texts.period: Legend told to Marco Polo c. 1270s; English: The Travels of Marco Polo (Marsden 1818 ed.); Persian sources of the 13th century

source.archive: Google Books (public domain scan of Marsden ed. 1818)
source.work: The Travels of Marco Polo, ch. on the Old Man of the Mountain (English, Marsden 1818 ed.); cf. Juvayni's Arabic-Persian history (13th century)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1818; Arabic-Persian originals 13th century)

summary.en: The Venetian traveller tells of the Old Man of the Mountain, Hasan-i Sabbah, who kept at Alamut a secret garden watered with milk and honey, with boys and girls of beauty, to which he brought his young men drugged with wine and hemp; they woke in 'Paradise' and were cast out again, believing their master could return them at will. Hence, the legend says, the obedience of the Assassins to death. Modern historians find the garden only in the Western tellings; the fortress itself was taken by the Mongols in 1256.
summary.zh: 威尼斯旅人所述山中老人哈桑·薩巴赫於阿拉穆特蓄一秘密花園，水以乳與蜜，藏絕色男女；以酒與麻藥之青年入園，醒於『樂園』，復被逐出，信其主可隨意使之復返。相傳刺客由此捨死聽命。現代史家謂此花園僅見於西方敘述；要塞本身於1256年被蒙古人攻陷。

sensitivity.note: A Western legend about a Muslim sect, recorded by Marco Polo and doubted by modern historians of the Nizari Isma'ilis; presented as a story about how the East was told in Europe, not as an established fact.

passages.text: Marco Polo tells of the Old Man of the Mountain, who kept at Alamut a secret garden: he had it watered with milk and honey, and filled it with boys and girls of marvellous beauty, with palaces and music and wine. Thither he brought the young men of his following drugged with wine and a herb, and they woke among the delights and believed they were in Paradise; and after a season he cast them out, saying that Paradise could be theirs again if they did his bidding.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the tale in The Travels of Marco Polo (Marsden ed. 1818); not verbatim.

passages.text: So, the legend says, the young men went to their deaths without fear, obedient to the smallest word of the Old Man — whence the name Assassins, from the hashish of the drug, in the European tellings. The historians of the Mongol conquest of 1256, and the modern students of the Nizari Isma'ilis, find nothing of the garden in the Persian sources; the tale is the West's romance about a fortress it feared, and it is told here as a story about stories.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the tale and of the historiographical caution; not verbatim.

title.en: Al-Hajjaj: The Vizier of the Iron Rod

region.zh: 伊拉克庫法與瓦西特（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Events 694-714 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 31
texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The caliph Abd al-Malik sends al-Hajjaj to Kufa with no force: he rides into the mosque hooded, unmasks, and speaks the speech the historians have kept — 'I am he who trims the feather and sharpens the point, I am the punishment of God among you.' The city is governed by terror for ten years; the dialect of the mosque is corrected by the rod; and at his death the caliph says the tribute the biographers remember: 'I raised him when he was light, and he made himself heavy.'
summary.zh: 哈里發阿布杜·馬利克不遣一兵而遣哈賈季至庫法：他蒙面入清真寺，揭面而言史家所存之句——『我是削羽磨鋒之人，我是降於你們中間的主之懲罰。』城中以恐怖為治十年；清真寺之語以棒正音；其死時，哈里發言傳記所存之語：『我提拔他時他尚輕，而他自任為重。』

sensitivity.note: Umayyad anecdote lore as gathered in Muir.

passages.text: The caliph Abd al-Malik sent al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf to Kufa without an army. He rode into the mosque hooded, on a mule, and sat; then he unmasked and spoke: 'I am he who trims the feather and sharpens the point; I am the punishment of God among you.' And he governed the city and then the East by terror for ten years, it is said, and slew more men than the wars of his time had taken.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 31; not verbatim.

passages.text: The anecdote lore keeps his sayings: that he corrected the reading of the mosque by the rod; that he called the men of Kufa 'the dregs of the Arabs'; and that at his death the caliph said of him: 'I raised him when he was light, and he made himself heavy.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 31; not verbatim.

title.zh: 穆塔瓦基勒與詩人的譴責

region.zh: 阿拔斯都城薩邁拉（實際定位）

texts.period: Events 847-861 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 50
texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The caliph al-Mutawakkil builds the great mosque of Samarra with its spiral minaret, keeps poets at his table, and dies of a court plot of his own son — the anecdote lore keeps the word said over him: 'He was the most magnificent of the caliphs and the most prodigal.' The Abbasid court at its height is here: the lute, the verses, the wine, and the sword behind the curtain.
summary.zh: 哈里發穆塔瓦基勒建薩邁拉大清真寺與其螺旋宣禮塔，蓄詩人於席，終死於其子主使之宮廷陰謀——軼事之集存其蓋棺之語：『他是最華麗的哈里發，也是最揮霍者。』阿拔斯宮廷之盛在此：琴、詩、酒，與幕後之劍。

sensitivity.note: Abbasid court anecdote lore as gathered in Muir.

passages.text: Al-Mutawakkil built the great mosque of Samarra, with its minaret wound like a screw into the sky, and kept the poets and singers of the age at his table. The anecdote lore remembers him as the most magnificent and the most prodigal of the caliphs: it was said that he built palaces without number and spent his nights in verse and wine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 50; not verbatim.

passages.text: He was slain in his sleep by the guard of his own court, at the instance of his son; and the histories write the moral of the Abbasid height: the lute, the verse, the wine — and the sword behind the curtain. And the great mosque of Samarra stood, the largest mosque of the age, its spiral minaret the landmark of the desert capital.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 50; not verbatim.
